\section{Berezin Integration (PSI QFT II, Tutorial 7)}

\noindent\textit{Question prompts paraphrased from the official
\href{https://psi-online.perimeterinstitute.ca/courses/take/quantum-field-theory-ii-student/pdfs/20776400-module-6-tutorial}{Perimeter PSI Online sheet};
the equations and notation follow the source.}

\subsection{Grassmann Variables}

Let $\theta_a$ and $\bar\theta_a$, with $a=1,\ldots,N$, be $N$ conjugate
pairs of Grassmann variables, and let $A$ be an $N\times N$ matrix. Begin
from the identity
\begin{equation}
    \int \prod_{a=1}^{N} d\bar\theta_a\,d\theta_a\,
    \exp\!\left[-\sum_{c,d}\bar\theta_c A_{cd}\theta_d\right]
    =\det(A).
\end{equation}

\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
    \item Introduce independent conjugate Grassmann sources $\bar\eta_c$ and
    $\eta_c$, which anticommute with one another and with every $\theta_a$ and
    $\bar\theta_a$. Show that
    \begin{equation}
        \begin{aligned}
        Z[\bar\eta,\eta]
        &=\int \prod_{a=1}^{N}d\bar\theta_a\,d\theta_a\,
        \exp\!\left[
            -\sum_{c,d}\bar\theta_cA_{cd}\theta_d
            +\sum_c\bigl(\bar\eta_c\theta_c+\bar\theta_c\eta_c\bigr)
        \right] \\
        &=\det(A)\exp\!\left[
            \sum_{c,d}\bar\eta_c(A^{-1})_{cd}\eta_d
        \right].
        \end{aligned}
    \end{equation}
    \begin{solution}
        We shift the integral measure by
        \begin{equation}
            \tilde{\theta}_a = \theta_a - A_{ab}^{-1}\eta_b.
        \end{equation}
        Then, the exponent becomes
        \begin{equation}
            \begin{aligned}
                -(\bar{\tilde{\theta}}_c + \bar{\eta}_bA_{bc}^{-1})A_{cd}(\tilde{\theta}_d + A_{da}^{-1}\eta_a) + \bar{\eta}_c(\tilde{\theta}_c + A_{ca}^{-1}\eta_a) + (\bar{\tilde{\theta}}_c + \bar{\eta}_bA_{bc}^{-1})\eta_c = -\bar{\tilde{\theta}}_cA_{cd}\tilde{\theta}_d+\bar{\eta}_cA_{cd}^{-1}\eta_d,
            \end{aligned}
        \end{equation}
        which follows
        \begin{equation}
            Z[\bar{\eta},\eta] = \det A \exp(\bar{\eta}_cA_{cd}^{-1}\eta_d).
        \end{equation}
    \end{solution}

    \item Use $Z[\bar\eta,\eta]$ and the differentiation rules for Grassmann
    variables to evaluate
    \begin{equation}
        \left\langle\theta_a\bar\theta_b\right\rangle
        =\frac{
            \displaystyle
            \int\prod_c d\bar\theta_c\,d\theta_c\,
            e^{-\bar\theta\cdot A\cdot\theta}\,
            \theta_a\bar\theta_b
        }{
            \displaystyle
            \int\prod_d d\bar\theta_d\,d\theta_d\,
            e^{-\bar\theta\cdot A\cdot\theta}
        },
        \qquad
        \left\langle\theta_a\theta_b\right\rangle.
    \end{equation}
    \begin{solution}
        Using
        \begin{equation}
            \frac{\partial Z[\bar{\eta},\eta]}{\partial \bar{\eta}_a} = \int \prod_{a=1}^{N}d\bar\theta_a\,d\theta_a\,\theta_a
        \exp\!\left[
            -\sum_{c,d}\bar\theta_cA_{cd}\theta_d
            +\sum_c\bigl(\bar\eta_c\theta_c+\bar\theta_c\eta_c\bigr)
        \right],
        \end{equation}
        and
        \begin{equation}
            -\frac{\partial Z[\bar{\eta},\eta]}{\partial \eta_b} = \int \prod_{a=1}^{N}d\bar\theta_a\,d\theta_a\,\bar{\theta}_b
        \exp\!\left[
            -\sum_{c,d}\bar\theta_cA_{cd}\theta_d
            +\sum_c\bigl(\bar\eta_c\theta_c+\bar\theta_c\eta_c\bigr)
        \right].
        \end{equation}
        We can write
        \begin{equation}
        \begin{aligned}
            \langle\theta_a\bar{\theta_b}\rangle &= -\frac{1}{Z[0,0]}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\bar\eta_a \partial\eta_b}Z[\bar{\eta}, \eta]\bigg|_{\eta=0}\\
            &=-\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\bar\eta_a \partial\eta_b}\exp(\bar{\eta}_cA_{cd}^{-1}\eta_d)\bigg|_{\eta=0}\\
            &=\frac{\partial}{\partial \bar \eta_a}\left[\bar \eta_c A_{cd}^{-1}\exp(\bar{\eta}_cA_{cd}^{-1}\eta_d)\right]\bigg|_{\eta=0}\\
            &= A_{cd}^{-1}.
        \end{aligned}
        \end{equation}
    \end{solution}

    \item Establish
    \begin{equation}
        \left\langle
            \theta_a\bar\theta_b\theta_c\bar\theta_d
        \right\rangle
        =(A^{-1})_{ab}(A^{-1})_{cd}
        -(A^{-1})_{ad}(A^{-1})_{cb},
    \end{equation}
    and explain how the two pairings and their relative sign realize Wick's
    theorem for fermions.
    \begin{solution}
        Using the same method, we have
        \begin{equation}
            \begin{aligned}
                \langle \theta_a \bar \theta_b \theta_c \bar \theta_d\rangle &= -\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\bar \eta_a\partial\eta_b}\left[A_{cd}^{-1} - \bar \eta_e A^{-1}_{ed}A_{cf}^{-1}\eta_f\exp(\bar{\eta}_cA_{cd}^{-1}\eta_d)\right]\bigg|_{\eta=0}\\
                &=A_{ab}^{-1}A_{cd}^{-1} - A_{ad}^{-1} A_{cb}^{-1}.
            \end{aligned}
        \end{equation}
        In terms of Wick's theorem, this is
\begin{equation}
    \begin{aligned}
        \langle \theta_a \bar\theta_b \theta_c \bar\theta_d\rangle&=\
                \wick{
            \c1{\theta_a}\c1{\bar\theta_b}\,
            \c2{\theta_c}\c2{\bar\theta_d}
        }
        +
\wick{
            \c2{\theta_a}\c1{\bar\theta_b}\,
            \c1{\theta_c}\c2{\bar\theta_d}
        }
        \\
        &=
        \wick{
            \c1{\theta_a}\c1{\bar\theta_b}\,
            \c2{\theta_c}\c2{\bar\theta_d}
        }
        -
        \wick{
            \c1{\theta_a}\c1{\bar\theta_d}\,
            \c2{\theta_c}\c2{\bar\theta_b}
        }
        \\
        &=
        A^{-1}_{ab}A^{-1}_{cd}
        -
        A^{-1}_{ad}A^{-1}_{cb}.
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
    \end{solution}
\end{enumerate}

Now take the continuum limit $\theta_a\to\psi_\alpha(x)$, where
$\alpha=1,2,3,4$ is a suppressed Dirac index, and replace $A_{cd}$ by the
integral kernel $A(x,y)$. Use
\begin{equation}
    \{\psi(x),\psi(y)\}=0,
    \qquad
    \frac{\delta\psi(x)}{\delta\psi(y)}=\delta^4(x-y).
\end{equation}

\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*),resume]
    \item In the finite-dimensional case, prove
    \begin{equation}
        \left\{\frac{d}{d\theta_a},\theta_b\right\}=\delta_{ab},
        \qquad
        \left\{\frac{d}{d\theta_a},\frac{d}{d\theta_b}\right\}=0,
    \end{equation}
    and write the corresponding functional relations for the Grassmann fields
    $\psi(x)$.
    \begin{solution}
        \begin{equation}
            \left\{\frac{d}{d\theta_a},\theta_b\right\}f(\theta) = \delta_{ab}f(\theta) - \theta_b \frac{df}{d\theta_a} + \theta_b \frac{df}{d\theta_a} = \delta_{ab}f(\theta) \quad \forall f(\theta).
        \end{equation}
        \begin{equation}
            \left\{\frac{d}{d\theta_a},\frac{d}{d\theta_b}\right\} = \frac{d}{d\theta_a}\frac{d}{d\theta_b} + \frac{d}{d\theta_b}\frac{d}{d\theta_a} = 0.
        \end{equation}
    \end{solution}

    \item Complete the continuum Gaussian identity
    \begin{equation}
        \begin{aligned}
        &\int\mathcal{D}\bar\psi\,\mathcal{D}\psi\,
        \exp\Bigg[
            -\int d^4x'\,d^4x\,
                \bar\psi(x')A(x',x)\psi(x) \\
        &\hspace{43mm}
            +\int d^4x\,
                \bigl(\bar\psi(x)\eta(x)+\bar\eta(x)\psi(x)\bigr)
        \Bigg]
        =\cdots .
        \end{aligned}
    \end{equation}
    \begin{solution}
         We can read this off directly from the finite version,
         \begin{equation}
             Z[\bar \eta,\eta ] = \det A'(x,x') \exp\left(\int d^dx \int d^dx'\bar \eta(x) A'^{-1}(x,x')\eta(x')\right).
         \end{equation}
    \end{solution}

    \item Determine the two-point correlation function when
    \begin{equation}
        A=i\gamma\cdot\partial-m.
    \end{equation}
    \begin{solution}
        \begin{equation}
        \begin{aligned}
            \langle \psi(x) \bar \psi(y)\rangle &= A'^{-1}(x,y) =\int \frac{d^dk}{(2\pi)^d}\frac{-e^{ik\cdot(x-x')}}{\slashed{k} + m}.
        \end{aligned}
        \end{equation}
    \end{solution}
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Gross--Neveu Model}

Consider the two-dimensional Gross--Neveu model
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GN}}
    =\bar\psi_a i\slashed{\partial}\psi^a
    +\frac{g^2}{2N}\bigl(\bar\psi_a\psi^a\bigr)^2,
\end{equation}
where $a=1,\ldots,N$ is a colour index and each suppressed Dirac index has
two values.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
    \item Find the mass dimension of $g$.
    \begin{solution}
        $[g] =0$.
    \end{solution}

    \item Choose
    \begin{equation}
        \gamma^0=\sigma^2,
        \qquad
        \gamma^1=i\sigma^1,
        \qquad
        \gamma^5=\gamma^0\gamma^1=\sigma^3.
    \end{equation}
    Show that $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GN}}$ is invariant under
    $\psi_a\mapsto\gamma^5\psi_a$, and explain why this symmetry excludes a
    fermion mass term.
    \begin{solution}
        Under the transformation
        \begin{equation}
            \bar \psi \gamma^\mu \psi \to \psi^\dagger \gamma^5\gamma^0 \gamma^\mu \gamma^5 \psi = \bar \psi\gamma^\mu\psi.
        \end{equation}
        This can be checked using explicit matrix multiplication. Meanwhile,
        \begin{equation}
            \bar \psi \psi = \psi^\dagger \gamma^0 \psi \to \psi^\dagger \gamma^5 \gamma^0 \gamma^5 \psi = - \psi^\dagger \gamma^0 = -\bar \psi \psi.
        \end{equation}
        Therefore, the Dirac mass is not allowed, and
        \begin{equation}
            (\bar \psi \psi)^2 \to (\bar \psi \psi)^2.
        \end{equation}
    \end{solution}

    \item Show that the model is equivalent to the auxiliary-scalar theory
    \begin{equation}
        \mathcal{L}_{\psi,\sigma}
        =\bar\psi_a(i\slashed{\partial}-\sigma)\psi^a
        -\frac{N}{2g^2}\sigma^2,
    \end{equation}
    where $\sigma(x)$ is a scalar field.
    \textit{Hint: perform the functional integral over $\sigma$.}
    \begin{solution}
        Integrating over the scalar field, we have
        \begin{equation}
            \begin{aligned}
                &\int \mathcal{D}\sigma\exp\left(- \int d^2x\bar\psi_a(i\slashed{\partial}-\sigma)\psi^a
        -\frac{N}{2g^2}\sigma^2\right)\\
        &=\exp\left(-\int d^2x\bar\psi_ai\slashed{\partial}\psi\right)\int \mathcal{D}\sigma\exp\left(-\int d^2x\left(\frac{N}{2}\frac{1}{g}\sigma + \frac{g}{\sqrt{2N}}(\bar\psi   _a\psi^a)\right)^2 + \frac{g^2}{2N}(\bar\psi   _a\psi^a)^2\right)\\
        &= \mathrm{const} \times \exp\left(-\int d^2x \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GN}}\right).
            \end{aligned}
        \end{equation}
    \end{solution}

    \item Instead perform the functional integral over $\psi$ and show that the
    model becomes the scalar-field theory
    \begin{equation}
        \mathcal{L}_\sigma
        =-\frac{N}{2g^2}\sigma^2
        +N\operatorname{tr}\log(i\slashed{\partial}-\sigma).
    \end{equation}
    \begin{solution}
        Integrating over the fermion fields, we have
        \begin{equation}
            \begin{aligned}
                &\int \mathcal{D}\bar \psi_a\mathcal{D}\psi_a \exp\left(- \int d^2x\bar\psi_a(i\slashed{\partial}-\sigma)\psi^a
        -\frac{N}{2g^2}\sigma^2\right)\\
        &=\exp\left(-\int d^2x - \frac{N}{2g^2}\sigma^2\right)\left(\int \mathcal{D}\bar\psi\mathcal{D}\psi\exp\left(- \int d^2x\bar\psi(i\slashed{\partial}-\sigma)\psi
        \right)\right)^N\\
        &=\exp\left(-\int d^2x - \frac{N}{2g^2}\sigma^2\right)\det(i\slashed{\partial}-\sigma)^N\\
        &=\exp\left(-\int d^2x - \frac{N}{2g^2}\sigma^2 +N\operatorname{tr}\log(i\slashed{\partial}-\sigma)\right).
            \end{aligned}
        \end{equation}
    \end{solution}
\end{enumerate}
